name: Name
body: Battle Forge is a monthly series that presents a new WARMACHINE scenario in each installment. Battle Forge scenarios emphasize the narrative unfolding over the course of a game and may be asymmetrical, uneven, and even somewhat experimental because the goal of Battle Forge is to create a sandbox toolset that allows for creative scenario generation and new, story-worthy experiences with WARMACHINE! Players are encouraged to modify Battle Forge scenarios in any way that makes the scenario more appropriate for their army collections and their available terrain resources. Most important of all, have fun! And if you find a better way to do something with a scenario that results in a better experience for you, let us know at feedback@privateerpress.com, so we can try it, too!

name: Name
body: Following are the key terms that will be repeated in many Battle Forge scenarios:

name: Name
body: Many scenarios utilize objectives. An objective can either be a terrain piece, a marker, or a zone designated on a terrain piece or on the map.

name: Name
body: Objective Markers are impassable terrain features and should be represented on the table with markers that are at least 20 mm in diameter. Unless otherwise specified, all Objective Markers used in a scenario should be the same size.

name: Name
body: To have more models in an area than your opponent does.

name: Name
body: An area or objective is contested if both players have models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective at a time when scoring would take place. An area or objective is uncontested if only one player has models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective when scoring would take place.

name: Name
body: The zone or the area of a terrain feature is held when a player occupies the area with two or more models, uncontested.

name: Name
body: An objective terrain piece or marker is secured when a player has two or more models within 1" of the objective, uncontested.

name: Name
body: Battle Forge victories can be determined by either achieving the goals of the scenario or through Victory Points, scored in a variety of ways throughout playing a scenario. Turn limits on scenarios put pressure on players to succeed within a set amount of turns, and Victory Points provide the means to determine victory when neither player has completed the primary objective of a scenario.

name: Name
body: In addition to its standard rules, each Battle Forge scenario has two random tables that add additional Victory Point-scoring opportunities for players that vary each time the scenario is played. Mission Modifiers add additional scoring opportunities based on the position of a player’s models on the table. Achievements add additional scoring opportunities based on a player’s actions taken on the battlefield. Players should roll a d6 to randomly determine Mission Modifiers and Achievements before the beginning of a game, or players can choose them at will if all players agree. It is recommended that only one Mission Modifier and one Achievement should be in effect during any match (unless you really want to get crazy).

name: Name
body: If a player makes an attack that destroys one or more friendly models, that player’s opponent gains 1 Victory Point. If a player makes an attack and destroys their own Leader model, that player immediately loses the match.

name: Name
body: In addition to objectives, Battle Forge scenarios will routinely draw on the following terrain elements. Dimensions provided are approximations, and you should feel free to substitute any terrain pieces you have available as necessary. Use the resources you have available to get close enough to maintain the spirit and intention of the scenario.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 3/4" x 4". Barriers provide cover.

name: Name
body: Obstructions with an approximate footprint of 5" x 5".

name: Name
body: Forest areas with an approximate footprint of 5" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 2" x 2". Small obstacles provide cover.

name: Name
body: An elevated platform at least 1" above the table, such as a hill or terrace. Plateaus can possess multiple areas at different heights that models can be placed on, but the areas must be level to prevent models from falling over. If a model cannot be placed on a level area without risk of falling off, it cannot occupy that area. Models cannot be placed on slopes, and we recommend that plateau terrain with sloped surfaces not be used. Hill, Small—A plateau platform with a footprint approximately 6" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 30 mm models to be placed on. Hill, Large—A plateau with a footprint approximately 6" to 12" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 40 mm models to be placed on.

name: Name
body: An area of shallow water approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An area of rubble approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: A 3" x 5" trench template.

name: Name
body: Two souls with but a single thought: destroy! The "Two Hearts That Beat as One" scenario utilizes the Duos format that we pioneered for the "For the Date Night" scenario. The Duos format allows you to build forces using two Leaders. Everything else about force building remains the same: each Leader must have at least one Cohort model in their battlegroup, you must take five Command Cards, etc. Note all Duos matches require that both players bring two Leaders to the battle. For the most part, gameplay remains the same as well, only now you’ll be managing two Leaders during each phase of your turns. However, Leaders can only allocate focus or reave fury from Cohort models in their own battlegroup. And the biggest difference is that when you lose one Leader, the game doesn’t end. Wading into the fray with a two-Leader force should not be undertaken lightly. You’re doubling up the most complicated models in your force. And this is highly experimental—that is, untested in MKIV. The myriad combos that might be possible between any two Leaders remains to be discovered, and you will no doubt find some egregiously broken ones. But that’s going to be the fun of it all!

name: Name
body: Duos can also be a fantastic way to introduce someone new to WARMACHINE, and it’s here we hope you’ll seize the opportunity. In a Duos game, you can assign a small portion of a force, or even just a Leader and a single Cohort model, to a novice player, who then can play alongside a more experienced player to learn the ropes. Being able to shadow an ally while learning the game can be much more enjoyable than plunging directly into head-to-head competition. So, make it a double-date night, and team up with some new players to show them how it’s done!

name: Name
body: "Two Hearts That Beat as One" is designed to be played as a Duos 50- or 75-point battle.

name: Name
body: "Two Hearts That Beat as One" ends after six rounds.

name: Name
body: Their life force bonded, the two Leaders, one for each force, share a common pool of damage points with the ability to allocate any damage received to either Leader at will. Players can use this bond strategically as they battle to control the Objectives in the center of the map. Meanwhile, an arcane storm closes in, progressively shrinking the safe areas on the map until both armies are forced together in a climactic showdown. Victory is assured to the team that secures the final Objective with a Leader at the end of the match.

name: Name
body: Control the final Active Objective with at least one Leader at the end of six rounds.

name: Name
body: The map shown below uses 6 Objectives, 2 forests, 2 small hills, 4 barriers, 1 medium building, and 1 large pond.  If you don’t have this exact assortment of terrain, use what you have to create a diverse environment with an emphasis on terrain that blocks line-of-sight across long distances.

name: Name
body:
This scenario uses Execution Mode.
Victory Points are shared by both players on a team.
Soul Bonded—When a Leader suffers damage, the controlling player can allocate the damage between the targeted Leader and the other Leader on their team in any way they choose. If a Leader has been destroyed, damage cannot be allocated to them. If a Leader is allocated damage while Vulnerable, they are destroyed.
Storm Eye—Beginning on the second round and at the beginning of each round thereafter, roll a d6 to determine the Active Objective, based on the Objectives shown on the map. When a team ends their turn securing the Active objective, they gain 1 Victory Point.
Each turn, the arcane storm closes in, shrinking toward the Active Objective. Beginning on the second round, models ending their activation with any part of their base outside the Storm Eye diameter suffer a POW 20 damage roll. The Storm Eye diameter changes each round:
• Round 2—20"
• Round 3—15"
• Round 4—10"
• Round 5—5"
• Round 6—3"

name: Name
body: Roll once on both the Mission Modifiers and Achievement tables.

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Mission Modifier for this match. 1. Heartburn—Models securing an objective suffer –2 ARM. 2. Bleeding Hearts—The Leader in each army with the least amount of damage boxes remaining gains Stealth, if they have lost at least one damage box. 3. Hearts Afire—While both Leaders in an army have half or less than their starting damage boxes, both Leaders gain boosted attack and damage rolls.

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Achievement for this match. 1. Straight Through the Heart—The first player to damage an enemy Leader gains 1 Victory Point. 2. Racing Heart—If a team is securing an objective that becomes the new Active Objective, they gain 1 Victory Point. 3. Hearts of Gold—At the beginning of the sixth round, each team gains 1 Victory Point for each Leader in their army with no marked damage boxes.

name: Name
body: Victory conditions are checked in the following order: Decisive Win: At the end of the sixth round, if a team is securing the Active Objective with a Leader model, they win the match. Point Advantage Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, if a player has 4 or more Victory Points than their opponent, they win the match. Last Leader Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, a player with the last Leader model in play wins the match. Victory Point Win: If neither player has a Leader in play at the end of any of the second player’s turns, the player with the most Victory Points wins the match.

name: Name
body: Try using Soul Bonded and Execution Mode in Duos matches using other scenarios to see how these can change your strategic approach to the game. Soul Bonded may seem simple on the surface, but it can dramatically change the survivability of a Leader model, allowing a player to take risks with their Leader that they might otherwise avoid, particularly when used during Execution Mode.
